The Bibliotheca, also called the Myriobiblos, "ten thousand books", is a 9th-century work by Photios, later patriarch of Constantinople. It is a set of 279 reviews of books he had read, written for his brother Tarasios. Photios says he wrote it before leaving on an embassy to the Arabs, perhaps in the 850s, though the date is debated.

The entries run from a line to many pages. They cover Christian writers and pagan ones: historians, orators, novelists and doctors. Photios sums up each book and often judges its style. For many ancient works the Bibliotheca is the only record we have. Much of what is known of the lost books of Diodorus Siculus, and of Ctesias on Persia and India, comes from his notes.

It shows how much ancient Greek writing was still on the shelves of 9th-century Constantinople, and how much has been lost since. It belongs to the same urge to collect as the Suda a century later.
